en: Having bowed to Gajānana, the bestower of boons, and the son of Girijā, I shall now proclaim the Vararuci-śikṣā, the primary cause of the Vedas. (1)
The *mātrikā* follows the calf; likewise, the *vatsānusāriṇī* follows after the calf.
The *pākavatī* consists of three-quarters [of a syllable], while the *pipīlikā* consists of only one quarter.
The *vatsānusṛti* begins with a short vowel, whereas the *vatsānusāriṇī* ends with one.
In the *pākavatī* [meter], both [the short and long syllables] are deficient; in the *dīrghābhayāpipīlikā*, they are excessive.
The rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*)—namely, prolation (*pluta*) and the *pragraha*—are not applied.
Others, however, maintain that its duration is one mora (*mātrā*), while there is an addition of a quarter-mora (*pāda*).
When a word for a direction is placed before [a word] denoting a Brāhmaṇa, it is desired that [the vowel] be raised;

furthermore, the wise should state that the elision and the prohibition [of doubling] are reversed. When a *visarga* preceded by the vowel *i* stands before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a consonant, [it becomes *ś*].
There, that which has not been attained is attained, and likewise, that which has already been attained is not attained again.
A sparrow [utters] two morae when speaking, a crow [utters] two morae, and a peacock [utters] three morae; this is certain, there is no doubt in this matter.
The vowels should be known as Brāhmaṇas; those which are the first, second, and third of the consonant groups (vargas) are likewise Kṣatriyas;
the last of the groups and the semivowels (antasthas) are Vaiśyas.

The *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, the *śūdras*, and the sibilants (*ūṣman*)—how then are the castes among the letters, such as the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and so forth? It is said that for the Brāhmaṇas, [the duration] would be only a quarter of their own time. (9–10)

Half of that applies to the Kṣatriyas and others; according to the vision of the scriptures, some say it pertains to all stages of life and all consonants. Likewise, in the Pitṛmedha, in the Sahādhyāya, and in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.
In this [Vedic] text, the letter *ḍ* preceded by *h* or *m* certainly possesses the quality of being "difficult to touch" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*).

(12) Furthermore, if that [letter] is described by the learned as being distinguished by sound (*śabdaviśiṣṭa*), then when it is to be elided (*utkārya*), the *udātta* accent would certainly result for the following vowel (*utka*). (13)

A doubling never occurs after the letter *ra* or the letter *ha*, nor ever after a second or a fourth letter of a consonant class; however, a fourth letter may be doubled by a preceding third letter, and a following letter may be doubled by a preceding first letter. 14.

One should not suppress the beginning, the end, or the middle with one's own articulatory organ (svākṣara). At the conclusion, the letters of the *tavarga* class belong to the root of the teeth; the *ādi* and *anta* [of the *tavarga*] are produced at the root of the teeth.
However, the letter *na* belongs to the half-foot, as does any [nasal] from its own class (*savargata*) when in conjunction (*saṃyoga*). 15–16.
In the case of an avagraha, the letter *na* is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
it occurs at the tip of the tongue and in the middle; these two are considered the two types.
[This applies] in the case of *anuṣṭubh* verses, at the beginning of a word, and in the case of conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*) and avagrahas. 17.

That which is to be known as "yaḥ" (the word *ya*) is remembered as "yo'nyaḥ" (the word *ya* followed by *anya*). Where there is a circumflex (*svarita*) immediately following an avagraha, one should know that it is *tirovirāma*, provided that the avagraha has been stated. 18–19.

*Kareṇu*, *karviṇī*, *hariṇī*, *hāritā*, and *haṃsapadā*—these five are to be known as the *svarabhaktis*. *Kareṇu* occurs in the conjunction of *ra* and *ha*; *karviṇī* occurs in the conjunction of *la* and *ka*.
The *hariṇī* occurs with the letters *ra* and *śa*; the *hāritā* occurs with the letters *la* and *śa*. That which is called *haṃsapadā* occurs with the letters *repha* (r) and *ṣa*.
Thus, the fivefold division is described. 21–22.
One employing the *svarabhakti* should avoid the three defects:
the *ikāra*, the *ukāra*, and likewise the *grasta* defect.
The *ṛk*, the pause (*virāma*), and the *svarabhakti* are proclaimed to be self-sufficient.
And indeed, devotion that is independent [of external objects] is called the seat of the Truth (Ṛta).
(24) When a circumflex (svarita) vowel occurs after a long vowel at the end of a word, it belongs to the preceding vowel; as in "doṣāvastor haviṣmate. (25)
A wise person should bring about the *pracaya* (protracted) accent for a portion following a short vowel from its own [original] tone,
due to the differentiation of wind, the differentiation of vowels, and the differentiation of forms;
and because of the sound "vāsa," the nasal (*nāsikya*) is obtained first in the throat.
In the *Kāṭhaka*, the *svarabhakti* is proclaimed as either independent or subordinate;
one should know that in some places it is *ekaśruti*, while in others the accent (*svara*) is recognized.
Thus, the *svarabhakti* is either independent or a subordinate element of the consonant.
A different vowel or a different accent is found in the five types of questions;
likewise, it is prescribed at the beginning of forest-verses (āraṇyakas), at the end of two [sections], and in three [types of passages].
At the pause (avasāna), there is monotony (ekaśruti), or it may be accented acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita).
Whether it be the *prakṛti* (original form) or the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination), everything indeed constitutes the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

Scholars state that the "low" (*nīcatva*) quality of the vowel preceding the final consonant may sometimes take that very same form, and sometimes it occurs at the beginning or in the middle [of the word]. 30–31.
Agni, Jātavedas, Sahojā, Ajira, and Prabhu—in whatever time all these oblations may be offered, one should recognize devotion therein; there is no doubt about this. 32.
Where a conjunction of the letters *śa* and *na* is mentioned,
in that place the letter *i* is recited by the Taittirīyas; however,
for the five Kāṭhaka schools as well as for the Mātharas and Niṣādas, it is the same.
Their prescribed application occurs only here and not elsewhere;

for example, the addition of the letter *ka* before the *k*-group according to the rule in the *Kāṭhaka*, and the non-trembling (*akampita*) of a vowel that precedes the letters *lopa* and *ukāra* when they stand between [vowels]. (34–35)

In the three preceding [consonants] and in the following *ṣa-ṣaha* [consonants], there is only the letter *r* and the vowel *u*; therefore, no *bhakti* (vowel-portion) exists there. Furthermore, after a vowel ending in *u*, the letter *r* and the vowel *u* remain together with the *ṣa-ṣa* [consonants].
And here, because of its true nature, the syllable *ukāra* will undoubtedly lead to devotion.
(37) They teach three modes of speech: the slow, the medium, and the fast.
They say that within these modes there is a distinction of action; the specific measure undergoes a transformation. (38)
In that case, there may be a gap and an insertion between two words;
one should recognize that the letter *ca* is proclaimed as such in the *Kāṭhaka*. Likewise, in the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) of a short *e*-vowel, there is an insertion before it.
One should know that the letter *cha* is recited there in the middle of the word.

Following the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*), the letter *ja*, the letter *ka* as a medial augment (*madhyamāgama*), the letter *ga*, the letter *ka*, and the letter *tha* follow in their respective order. 40–41.
It is stated that in certain instances, there is no doubling of a consonant following a vowel;
rather, the first [consonant] of the second or fourth [class] is inserted as an augment (āgama) in the middle.
However, for the second [consonant] of the *tavarga*, the tip of the tongue is prescribed by the wise.
Because of its connection with that [ṣ], the letter ṣa is traditionally known as having little breath (alpapraṇa).

For the second [sibilant] preceded by ṭa, the tip of the tongue is said by the wise to be the point of articulation; its connection is indeed with śa and ṣa, and it is traditionally known as having little breath.
Of those two [groups], the first of the consonant classes (varga) and the second [class]—and also in the case of *ṣa* and *sa*—the wind is said to be the lesser; there is no doubt in this matter.
(45) Furthermore, in the case of the *ta*-class which is to be described hereafter, if it occurs at the beginning of a word...
The tip of the tongue is traditionally taught as the instrument for both *canā* and *mardhyai*.

However, that [tip] is not intended by the scripture to be the contact point for the lower portion; rather, its connection with those contacts is considered to be the maintenance of the preceding [sound] within the mouth. 46–47.

Just as the sounds *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* reach the nose through a gentle breath, so too the *ṣ* sound is not carried [to the palate] by him; rather, its correct placement is indeed [at the root of the tongue]. Therefore, the combined sound following the *ś* is not reached at the palate before the preceding one.
The prohibition regarding a conjunction [of consonants] when mixed with a sibilant (*ūṣman*) is not intended to apply there;
rather, there would be a mere division (*bhakti*) resulting from the substitution, and its status as a prior member is prescribed.
However, it is recited in the *Taittirīya* that this division belongs to the *lakāra*. 49–50.

He who exerts effort toward sacrificial acts alone in every way, and not elsewhere, is remembered as Aum, whose throat and other parts are [the letters]. (51) Furthermore, some maintain that effort (*prayatna*) is a distinct entity and is not accepted as being present everywhere.
One must always exert effort regarding the phonemes, vowels, and so forth;

by no means should there be doubling of that which precedes the *ṛ*-vowel. Furthermore, those who are devoid of the study of words will fail to understand the position and location of the words. 52–53.
They attain a pause (*virāma*) consisting of six morae (*ṣaṭpāda*); there is no doubt in this matter.
When there is a conjunction of vowels (*īcya*) and consonants (*padya*), the pause is traditionally recorded as being of one mora (*mātrika*).
Whether it takes two forms or three forms, it is indeed obtained within the sentence itself.
In each and every such instance, only the measure (mātrā) is spoken.
Whether a *ra* or a *ta* is seen, or where a guttural (*ka*-varga) appears, the connection with a vowel-quality (*guṇa*) at the joints [of the breath] is declared; of this there is no doubt. 55–56.
The wise person should recite while mentally recalling what is prescribed in the manuals on hand-gestures;
therefore, an intelligent man should avoid indicating [the letters] with his hand.
One should not release the breath through the nostrils during the conjunction of the *ha* sound.
One should not pronounce the *uras* (chest) sound as nasal (*ānada*) in the case of *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*.
(58) That which is *aurasya* (chest-born) exists at the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, but it is not seen in the *saṃhitā-pāṭha*.
(59) Therefore, if a wise person perceives its presence in the *saṃhitā*, there is no division [between the two].
In each respective case, the wise one should state that [application] as being absolute;
otherwise, it should also be explained according to the scripture and in accordance with the prescribed rule,
provided that what was previously infinite becomes finite later on.

Therein, that which stands in the middle is called the place of the nose; for when conjoined with the five [vowels], they are indeed known as the *yamās*. That which is equal to *a* is proclaimed as the throat-binding (*galabandha*).
If a sound is heard, or if there is a pause or a transposition;

or if a nasalized sound (*anunāsika*) or a *nāsikya* arises according to the form of the letter; or if it is joined with the end of a consonant class (*vargānta*), or with the sibilants (*ṣa-sa*), or even with the semivowels (*antaḥstha*). (63–64)
Having observed the *yamakas*, one should practice with extreme subtlety;
having transcended the seven notes (*svaras*), the *svarita* occurs in certain places. Its breath-force is slight, and it is traditionally known as having a "footed" movement (*pādavṛtti*). 65.
The third [note] of the *mandra* and others is declared by the wise to be "intense" (*nitānta*).
Thus it is seen in another treatise; therefore, when a semivowel (*antasthā*) arises first, the fifth [note] is uttered twice. (66–67)
When followed by *itarā* and so forth, that [accent] is not [perceived] there; thus it is remembered by the wise.
At the end of a pause (*avasāna*), a high-pitched (*udātta*) vowel is desired to become low-pitched (*nīca*) in sandhi.
This is likewise observed at the beginning of *āraṇya* and so forth, as well as at the end of two [words]. 68. Thus it is seen.
Regarding the svarita and udātta tones, as well as the svarita in cases such as *svapṛcchā* and so forth, the function of the anudātta resulting from their accumulation (*pracaya*) is now described:
first there is a strong [breath], then the air [is emitted] strongly for the subsequent [syllable]. (69–70)
For another [consonant], there should be a gentle breath (*maṃdavāyu*) applied according to the sequence;
where a conjunction of the letter *ha* with the *visarga* is observed, one should know that the effort (*prayatna*) therein is the same as it is for the [corresponding] class (*varga*). 71.
In the *ārṣeya* section of the Taittirīyas, the recitation is desired according to the [following] rules: one should recite two words from the beginning of each *anuvāka*;
and one should not speak from one *praśna* to another unless there is a causal connection between them.
In this chapter, those [vowels] enumerated by the Taittirīyas in the intervals between words and sentences should be employed; by that means they attain their goal.
Having transcended the *prāpti* vowels, the *iṣṭa* vowel remains.
According to the specific Upaniṣad, however, there is indeed the path for the six [vowels].
Among the labials and the vowels, one should perform the doubling with the first [consonant]; but for the two labials of the sixth [group], the doubling should by no means take place.
If a separation between those two labial vowels is observed, it does not exist for them even over time; likewise,
where the letter *pa* is seen between two labial vowels.

If the vowels had different forms and sounds, there would be no distinction between those two [vowels and consonants]. However, wherever a conjunction of vowels with the *vargottama* [consonants] is observed, the connection of the vowel *ai* with a nasal (*anunāsika*) does not exist. 78–79.
But in that which is not of Ṛṣi origin, whatever function is common should be shared;
no specific distinction is desired there, except for those [rites] remembered as mantras and so forth.
There are eight endings, but the Gaurī and Āgneya [endings] alone [are used].
Having completed [the recitation], I performed it there when a word followed with the *udātta* accent (81); likewise, I performed the specific [recitation] "sūryaśca" in my mind,
honoring the *devapāṭha* as well as that which pertains to the gods (82).
Therefore, one should abandon [the word] *udātta* and others, but one should not abandon others either;
for by this [rule], Agni is intended to be expressed by words such as *mahi* in the Vedas.
Likewise, the word *tam u stotāraḥ*, *dūrvā*, and *duḥsvapna* [are also intended]. 83.
In that case, the preceding *s* also undergoes the change to *ṣ* due to *saṃhitā*.
(84) *Jyotis*, *āyus*, the *visarga*, *vṛddhi*, and *dharṣatva*—thus, the form of the short vowel is to be understood through these four. (85)
One should know that the long vowel is double [the duration] of the short, and the protracted (pluta) is triple;
it should be employed with the color of the stage, and one should not swallow the preceding syllable.
One should employ the long vowel first, and afterwards perform the nasalization (nāsikya).
That which arises from the heart, beautiful and remembered as having a sound like bronze,
possessing two moras and three moras, and being accompanied by nasality— these are proclaimed as the designations for the *nāda* (resonance) of the final letters of each consonant class. 87–88.
This *nāda* is the letter *ha*, and these are remembered as the qualities of the phonemes;
the connection with the touch (*sparśa*) of the *praṇava* is not intended there. There, the vowel measure (*mātrā*) is the letter *va*; of this there is no doubt.
In the Ṛgveda and in its divisions, the *praṇava* is employed at the beginning;
during the third part of the morning, it should not be placed in the middle of two parts.
One should always place the *praṇava* of Brahman at both the beginning and the end.
That which is not performed first flows away, and that which is not performed last falls apart;
likewise, the Vedas begin with the *praṇava* and are established within the *praṇava*.
Since the entire *praṇava* consists of speech, one should therefore practice the *praṇava*.

Just as butter might be found within curd, or as [the breath] residing in the throat might be perceived by us through effort, so too should one perceive the unmanifest vowels that have entered the audible ones;
having moved from one vowel to an equivalent vowel with a smooth transition, one should follow its euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) without harshness. 93–94.
One should make it equal to a severed [line], like a subtle shadow or heat;
when joined with the word "eva," its original nature is not intended there.
One should know that this has attained a secondary quality (guṇa), as proclaimed in the Kāṭhaka.
In that case, a negation conjoined with another word by means of sound is not accepted;
one should understand that what is established there is how the action proceeds.
The wise declare that for the third [note] among the *maṃdra* and others, it is extremely [high]. 96–97.

Thus it is seen in another treatise; therefore, [the substitution] proceeds intensely for the *pragraha*, the *upasarga*, and likewise for the compound. In the middle, the substitutes are [the *guṇa* vowels], and the augmentations are the *i*-vowel and *u*-vowel for the sounds *ya* and *va*.
In the *Kāṭhaka*, the *pitrya* [sandhi] is proclaimed after *rātryāḥ*, *maṃtrya*, *pitryoḥ*, and *bhartryoḥ* from their respective bases (*dhiṣṇyāt*).
Indeed, no one who speaks the Veda ever uses an anusvāra preceded by the vowel *ā*;
this is seen as a *saṃhitā*-form for the sake of the following *ṛ*. Therefore, [the rule] "after a word" (*śabdāt*) is equal to "from a base" (*parassamaḥ*). 99–100.
In the chapter of the Taittirīyas, the *svarita* accent may arise during the day;

it should be employed with the breath (*āgrena*), and the wise one should recite it with a sharp, swift force, as if hurried by a violent wind. 101. The wise one should indeed utter the *svarita* with intensity.

The ninth [chapter] concerning Vāyukarṇa arises; there is no doubt in this matter. At the beginning, a single revelation shines forth, but afterwards there is no lineage. There is no further [revelation]; indeed, both the vow and the revelation shall be the revelation itself. 102–103.
In the case of a conjunction with a combined *ūṣman*, a prohibition is not intended there;
one should understand that there is a figurative application (*bhakti*) in that instance, and the status of being a prior member (*pūrvāṅgatva*) is prescribed.
In that context, the *repha* of a two-mora vowel [becomes] half a mora after [the vowel] other than *ṛ*.

When half of a visarga is proclaimed to be one mātrā, it becomes three mātrās in teaching; and that same [mātrā] applies to the syllable *mātrikā*. Wherever a *nakāra* preceded by *repha* (r) is seen at the end of a word, [it is treated as such]. 105–106.

One should recognize the distinction therein; this is called "duality. When a cat torments its own offspring with its mouth and its claws, by such an application of color (or syllable), one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One should not squeeze the kitten with one's mouth, nor with the teeth.
(108) He who does not utter the sequence of syllables is the cause of his being a cat;
just as a tiger might carry off its cub, yet should not bite it with its fangs. (109)
Fearing both falling and breaking, one should pronounce the phonemes in that same manner;
one should know it to have two morae (mātrās), and by no means three.
At the end of the animal [syllable], that which was taught in the previous scripture must not be uttered under any circumstances.
Therefore, one should avoid that which is hurried in its recitation.
When vowels and consonants are constantly applied even by the measure of a minute atom, the cognition of the *mātrā* is proclaimed to arise from the abundance of such combinations. 111–112.
In all instances, the *svāhākāra* should indeed be either udātta or svarita;
however, in the two *anuvākas* concerning Sūrya and Agni in the Kāṭhaka, it shall be only anudātta-udātta.
As for that which will be mentioned later in the Kāṭhaka, it is prescribed as being level in the middle.
The *lopakāra* (elision) should be performed, and the *varja* (avoidance) is indeed well-observed.

The *prasāda* is the Veda itself, and it is traditionally remembered as having a long measure (*dīrghamātra*). The *anusvāra* should be understood [as one measure], while the *vṛñjana* has half a measure (*ardhamātraka*). 114–115.
When there is loss of syllables, modification, or inversion, then the *sākṣa* itself is the authority; if there is no specific distinction here, there is no doubt.
Furthermore, if the *Śīkṣā* and the *Prātiśākhya* should come into conflict, [the former prevails]. 116.
If there is a *balisvara* in the *Prātiśākhya*, provided it is not the letter *da*,
that specific form which follows the number ten is indeed intended to be understood as a particular case, even without further qualification. (117–118)

In the *bhūr* and other mantras, within the five [syllables] beginning with the sentence, there is neither a vowel nor a harsh sound following the letter *ha*; one should not perform a sandhi when preceded by *su*, *vi*, *nṛ*, or *m*. Wherever the vowels of the preceding and succeeding parts undergo modification, and where the preceding [vowel] is a sibilant (*ūṣman*) standing before a subsequent [consonant], [the rule applies].

The dissolution of the preceding vowel is proclaimed as *svarabhakti*. Sound is heard from a voiced consonant (*ghoṣa*), and likewise from a pause (*virāma*) or a doubled consonant (*dvitva*). Then, from the form of the phoneme (*varṇa*), both the non-nasal (*anāsika*) and the nasal (*nāsikya*) arise. (120–121)
If, however, upon the mutual conjunction of consonants, there should occur that [nasal] which belongs to the preceding [vowel], and there is neither a hiatus nor a following consonant,
then a quarter-measure (pāda) is required for the nasalized sound situated between the manifest vowels, according to its own duration. 122.
For at that very moment, such a manifestation is attained; of this there is no doubt.
Time is said to be threefold: that which pertains to the indivisible word (*akhaṇḍapada*), that which pertains to the phonemes (*varṇa*), and that which pertains to the pauses (*virāma*). 123–124.
For the purpose of practice, one should employ a rapid tempo; for the purpose of performance, a medium tempo;
and for the purpose of instruction to disciples, one should employ a slow tempo—possessing both sequential and leaping movements, neither too fast nor too slow. (125)
One should speak that which is endowed with low, high, and natural tones, possessing speed and evenness.
Therein lie heaviness, lightness, and evenness; short, long, and protracted vowels; as well as elision, augmentation, and modification; and likewise natural state, valor, and sequence. 126–127.

The qualities of circumflex (svarita), acute (udātta), and grave (nīca) tones, as well as breath (śvāsa), resonance (nāda), and their combination— all this must be understood by one who studies the language of the Vedic meters (chandobhāṣā).
One should pronounce the phonemes in such a way that they are neither too distinct nor too indistinct.
"Like a wise man taking away immortality as if it were full of milk"—
thus ends the Vararuci-śikṣā.
